passage: On the rain-soaked bus to the science museum, the bus crawled through traffic and the windows fogged up. Siddharth told the whole back row, “I once saw a snake as long as this bus!” Pradeep laughed. “As long as this bus? Really?” “Okay, maybe as long as the aisle,” Siddharth grinned, waving both arms. “No, maybe as long as my arm.” The whole row was giggling now. Their teacher looked back and smiled. “That snake keeps getting shorter!” Siddharth said, “It was a tiny one, but it felt long.” Pradeep said, “I'd like to see that snake.” Everyone laughed.

qa.q: What did Siddharth claim to have seen that was as long as the bus?
qa.a: A snake.

qa.q: How was Siddharth feeling while shrinking the snake, and how can you tell there was no wish to deceive?
qa.a: Siddharth was cheerful and enjoying the joke, grinning and waving both arms while the row giggled, and admitted the snake was tiny.

qa.q: Why did the exaggeration work as a joke?
qa.a: Everyone in the row shared the joke and knew the snake was not really that long.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Siddharth's story?
qa.a: The teacher smiled and joined in, so probably saw it as harmless fun on a slow, wet ride.

grounding: A child exaggerates a tall tale for effect, and it is play rather than lying when both sides share the joke.

passage: “I ate a million rotis at Nani's house,” Jatin told Ramesh at the kitchen table, patting his stomach. Ramesh raised an eyebrow. “A million?” “Well, about a thousand.” Ramesh snorted. “You'd be bigger than a house.” Jatin puffed out his cheeks. “I was the biggest boy in the whole world!” They both cracked up. Ramesh's mother, cutting an onion, said, “I only made six, and half of them fell on the floor.” Jatin laughed even harder. “Okay, maybe two.” Ramesh grinned. “Exaggerating is your best trick.” Jatin bowed in his chair.

qa.q: How many rotis did Ramesh's mother say she made?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Jatin keep changing the number of rotis?
qa.a: Jatin was playing with the truth for fun, enjoying the joke, and both children knew it was not real.

qa.q: What makes this exaggeration different from lying?
qa.a: Both boys share the joke and know it is not real, and Jatin quickly admits a smaller number.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother have seen the tall tale?
qa.a: She joined in with a joke of her own, so she probably enjoyed it as harmless play.

grounding: A child exaggerates for effect, I ate a million rotis, playing with truth while both sides share the joke.

passage: “Guess how many golgappas I ate at the wedding.” Gurpreet leaned back like a king. “Ten?” said Chandrika. “A THOUSAND.” “A thousand!” “The golgappa man had to call for backup. Three more golgappa men came in a truck.” Chandrika snorted. “And then?” “Then I floated home like a balloon, and Mummy tied me to the gate with a string.” Chandrika was laughing too hard to talk. When she could, she said, “How many really?” Gurpreet grinned. “Eleven. But the thousand is the better story.” “It is,” said Chandrika. “Tell it at lunch tomorrow. Everyone will want the truck part.”

qa.q: How many golgappas did Gurpreet really eat?
qa.a: Gurpreet really ate eleven golgappas.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling while telling the story?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt playful and pleased, enjoying making Chandrika laugh with the tall tale.

qa.q: What shows the tall tale wasn't a lie?
qa.a: Both knew it was a joke, and when Chandrika asked, Gurpreet gave the real number straight away.

qa.q: How did Chandrika enjoy the story?
qa.a: Chandrika laughed too hard to talk and joined in, knowing it was a shared joke 😄

grounding: Shows a child's playful exaggeration that both friends know is not real, which makes it a story rather than a lie.

passage: I'm Nazia. I love silly stories. Last year I told the class I'd been chased to school by a tiger wearing sunglasses. Everyone laughed, because they know me. But Afreen was new, and she went pale. At break she asked, very seriously, whether the tiger was still near the bus stop, because her little sister walks there. My stomach dropped. For me it was obviously a joke. For her it wasn't. I told her straight away: “No tiger. I made it up for fun. Sunglasses, remember?” She laughed, a bit shakily. Now, when there's someone new, I make the story extra ridiculous, or I wink at the end, so everyone's in on it.

qa.q: What was the tiger in Nazia's story wearing?
qa.a: The tiger was wearing sunglasses.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she asked about the bus stop?
qa.a: Afreen felt worried and scared for her little sister, because she believed the tiger story.

qa.q: What did Nazia do to keep tall tales from becoming lies?
qa.a: Nazia told Afreen the truth straight away and now makes stories extra silly or winks, so everyone knows it's a joke.

qa.q: How did the rest of the class hear the tiger story?
qa.a: They laughed, because they know Nazia's silly stories and understood it was a joke.

grounding: Shows a child's tall tale being a shared joke for those who know, and needing a clear signal so it is not mistaken for a lie.

passage: Weekend-news note, Monday. Shalini, Class 3. Wasim told the class he built a rocket from cardboard boxes and flew to the moon, where he had lunch with an alien called Bob. He was grinning the whole time and made rocket noises. Two children shouted, “Liar!” Wasim's grin faded. I stepped in. “Is it a lie, or a story? What do you think Wasim wanted?” One girl said, “To make us laugh.” Wasim nodded hard. “And the rocket's real! It's in my room. It just doesn't fly.” I told the class that a tall tale everyone knows is pretend is a story, not a lie. Tomorrow Wasim is bringing the rocket.

qa.q: What was the alien called in Wasim's story?
qa.a: The alien was called Bob.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when the children shouted “Liar!”?
qa.a: Wasim felt hurt and deflated, his grin fading, since he only meant to make them laugh.

qa.q: How did Shalini help the class tell a tall tale from a lie?
qa.a: She asked what Wasim wanted, and explained that a story everyone knows is pretend is not a lie.

qa.q: What did the girl who answered understand about Wasim?
qa.a: She understood that Wasim wanted to make them laugh, not to trick them.

grounding: Shows a child's tall tale told for effect, and a teacher explaining that shared pretend is different from lying.

passage:
Saturday night
Today at Ganga's birthday I told everyone I ate a thousand gulab jamuns, my stomach turned into a hot-air balloon, and I floated over the whole building. Ganga laughed so hard her juice came out of her nose. Then she said she ate two thousand and flew to the moon, and the moon was made of rasmalai 😆 We kept going till her Nani said the ceiling fan would chop us if we floated any higher.
But little Tinku, who is four, asked me very seriously if my tummy still hurt. So I told him, "No, it's a pretend story. I only ate three." He looked relieved and went back to his cake.
Irfan

qa.q: How many gulab jamuns did Irfan really eat?
qa.a: Only three.

qa.q: Why did Irfan tell Tinku it was a pretend story?
qa.a: Irfan felt concerned when Tinku looked worried, and wanted Tinku to know the truth; the tale was only fun while everyone knew it was a joke.

qa.q: What made Irfan's exaggeration play rather than a lie?
qa.a: Everyone at the party knew it was silly and joined in, and when Tinku didn't share the joke, Irfan cleared it up at once.

qa.q: How was the tall tale different for Ganga than for Tinku?
qa.a: Ganga was in on the joke and delighted, adding her own moon story; Tinku didn't share it, so it felt like a real worry until Irfan explained.

grounding: It shows a child telling a tall tale for fun, a friend joining the shared joke, and the child making clear it is not real to a younger child who took it seriously.
